notes.meaning: Once the violent riot in Ephesus had quieted down, Paul called the believers together to encourage them. He embraced them warmly, said his goodbyes, and set out on the journey to Macedonia. Even after facing real danger, his main concern was to strengthen the local believers before moving on.

Paul travelled through the towns of Macedonia, spending much time teaching and encouraging the disciples along the way. After finishing that circuit, he journeyed south and arrived in Greece. His visits were always focused on building up the churches through thorough preaching.

Paul stayed three months in Greece, mostly visiting Corinth and the surrounding region. When he was just about to board a ship for Syria, he discovered a plot by hostile Jewish opponents to ambush or kill him. To protect his life and work, he wisely changed his route and returned by land through Macedonia.

A group of trusted Christian companions travelled with Paul as far as the province of Asia. These men represented churches from Berea, Thessalonica, Derbe, and Asia, showing the unity of believers across many regions. They were likely appointed by their home churches to help carry and deliver the relief offering for needy believers in Jerusalem.

These representatives went ahead of Paul and waited for the rest of the group at the port town of Troas. The writer uses the word 'us' here, showing that Luke had now rejoined Paul on the journey. Christian friends often planned ahead so they could travel together safely.

Paul and Luke sailed from Philippi after the spring Feast of Unleavened Bread had ended. Facing slow travel or opposing winds, it took five days to sail across to Troas to rejoin their companions. Once reunited, the entire missionary team stayed in Troas for a full week.

The believers gathered together on Sunday, the first day of the week, to share the Lord's Supper and worship. Because Paul planned to leave the next morning, he preached a long farewell sermon that lasted until midnight. The believers were so eager to hear God's word that nobody complained about the late hour.

differ.view: Some evangelicals believe the disciples gathering 'to break bread' on the first day of the week establishes a required biblical pattern for taking the Lord's Supper every Sunday.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern interpreters hold that if Luke used Jewish timekeeping, where a new day starts at sunset, this meeting was held on Saturday evening rather than Sunday evening.

notes.meaning: The church was gathered in an upstairs room that was brightly lit by many burning oil lamps. These lamps provided needed light for the nighttime meeting, though they also added to the heat and stuffiness of the crowded room. The bright light also ensured that their meeting was completely open and free from any suspicion of secret misconduct.

A young man named Eutychus was sitting on an open window sill, trying to listen as Paul spoke for hours. Eventually overcome by exhaustion and the warm room, he fell into a deep sleep. He lost his balance, fell three stories to the ground below, and was picked up dead.

Paul rushed downstairs immediately, threw himself across the young man's body, and embraced him in prayer. He then told the terrified crowd not to panic, reassuring them that the young man was alive. God worked through Paul's prayer to restore life to Eutychus just as He had through the ancient prophets Elijah and Elisha.

Paul went back upstairs, broke bread to eat, and resumed his warm conversation with the believers until the sun rose. Even after such a dramatic accident and miracle, he spent every remaining moment teaching them until dawn. When day broke, he finally set out on his journey.

The believers experienced great relief and joy as they were able to take the young man home alive and well. This amazing miracle confirmed Paul's preaching and turned their sudden sorrow into praise. It showed them God's tender care for their congregation.

Luke and the rest of the travel group boarded a ship to sail around the cape to the coastal city of Assos. Paul arranged to meet them there because he preferred to walk the shorter land route on foot. This gave Paul valuable quiet time for personal prayer and meditation before the trials that lay ahead.

Paul met up with his companions at Assos just as they had planned, and they took him back on board the ship. From there, they sailed together to Mitylene, an important port town on the island of Lesbos. Reunited with his friends, Paul continued his voyage toward Judea.

Continuing southward along the coast, the ship sailed past the island of Chios on the next day. The day after that they reached Samos, anchored near Trogyllium, and arrived at the ancient seaport of Miletus the following day. Luke records each stage of this journey with the accurate memory of an eyewitness traveller.

Paul purposely chose to sail past Ephesus without stopping there so he would not be delayed in the province of Asia. He was in a hurry to reach Jerusalem in time for the Feast of Pentecost, if at all possible. That feast would bring large crowds of worshippers together, giving him a wonderful opportunity to preach the gospel.

While stopping at Miletus, Paul sent a messenger about thirty miles to Ephesus to ask the church elders to come and meet him. These elders were the local pastors who had been appointed to care for and guide the Ephesian believers. Because he could not go to them, he called them to him for one last meeting.

differ.view: Anglicans teach that while 'elder' and 'bishop' are used interchangeably here, the later office of a bishop having oversight over local elders continues the apostolic authority shown by Paul.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic teaching holds that 'elder' or 'presbyter' names the ordained priestly office, while 'overseer' or 'bishop' describes their duty to watch over the congregation.

notes.meaning: When the elders arrived, Paul reminded them of the kind of life he had lived among them from the first day he set foot in Asia. His daily conduct had been consistent, honest, and completely open to everyone. A faithful teacher's life must always match the message he preaches.

Paul carried out his ministry with genuine humility, never seeking worldly honour or boasting in his position. He shed many tears of deep concern for souls, while enduring painful trials caused by hostile plots against his life. Even when enemies tried to stop his work, he stayed faithful to the Lord Jesus.

Paul never held back any truth that would help the believers grow spiritually, even if that truth was hard to hear. He taught the good news both in large public meetings and in private homes, going from house to house. A true pastor cares for people in personal visits just as much as from the pulpit.

Paul preached the very same message to everyone, whether they were Jews or Gentiles. He urged all people to repent—which means turning away from sin to follow God—and to put their complete trust in the Lord Jesus Christ. These two things, repentance toward God and faith in Jesus, are the core of the gospel.

Paul told the elders that he was now going to Jerusalem because he felt strongly led and bound by the Holy Spirit to do so. He did not know the exact details of what would happen to him once he arrived. True faith means obeying God's call even when the future is unknown.

The only thing Paul knew for certain was that the Holy Spirit gave him repeated warnings through Christian prophets in town after town. These messages made it clear that chains, prison, and suffering were waiting for him in Jerusalem. Yet knowing this danger did not cause him to shrink back from his duty.

Paul declared that his physical life had no supreme value to him compared to pleasing his Master. His only goal was to finish his race well and complete the ministry given to him by the Lord Jesus, which was telling people the good news of God's undeserved kindness. Finishing God's assignment faithfully mattered far more to him than staying safe.

Paul solemnly told the elders that none of them would ever see his face again in this life. He had spent years among them proclaiming the kingdom of God, but that chapter of his ministry was now closing forever. This painful reality made his final instructions all the more important.

Paul called them to witness on that very day that he was completely innocent of the spiritual ruin of any person. Like a faithful watchman on a city wall who sounds the alarm when danger approaches, he had warned everyone fairly. If anyone rejected the message and was lost, it would not be because Paul failed to warn them.

Paul could claim complete innocence because he had not shrunk back from teaching the whole plan and counsel of God. He did not pick and choose only the easy or pleasing parts of Scripture, but delivered the entire truth plainly. A faithful minister never hides God's truth just to stay popular.

Paul commanded the elders to guard their own spiritual lives first, and then to care for the whole flock entrusted to them. The Holy Spirit had made them overseers to shepherd the church of God, which is infinitely precious because the Lord bought it with His own blood. Church leaders must take their responsibility seriously because believers were purchased at such an enormous cost.

differ.view: Reformed Christians understand the statement that Christ purchased the church with His blood as teaching that He died to redeem a specific chosen people, the church.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern scholars note that ancient manuscripts vary between 'church of God' and 'church of the Lord,' and some translate the final phrase as 'the blood of His own Son.'

notes.meaning: Paul warned that after he departed, dangerous false teachers would break into the church like savage wolves attacking sheep. These outsiders would have no mercy on the congregation, seeking only to devour and harm the people. Pastors must always be on guard against dangerous errors coming from outside the fold.

Even more painfully, false teachers would arise from within their own congregation, and perhaps even from among the elders themselves. These men would twist God's truth to gain followers for themselves and cause bitter divisions. Pride and the desire to control others are the root cause of many heresies.

Paul told the elders to stay awake, alert, and watchful against these threats. He reminded them that for three full years he had never stopped warning each one of them, day and night, with tears of genuine love. His own tireless watchfulness was the pattern they were now called to follow.

Knowing he had to leave, Paul placed the elders into the loving care of God and the comforting message of His grace. That divine message has the power to build believers up in their faith and give them an eternal inheritance among all who are made holy. God's word is the sure anchor that keeps the church safe when human leaders depart.

Paul reminded them that he had never set his heart on anyone's silver, gold, or fine clothes while ministering in Ephesus. He had served the people with pure, unselfish motives rather than using religion for personal gain. A true servant of Christ must always guard against the snare of greed.

The elders knew from their own observation that Paul used his own hands to earn a living through the hard work of tentmaking. He worked early and late to provide food and clothing not only for himself, but also for his travelling companions. He refused to be a financial burden to the church he was trying to reach.

Through his own hard work, Paul showed the elders that believers ought to labour diligently so they can help the poor, sick, and vulnerable. He reminded them of a famous saying spoken by the Lord Jesus Himself: it brings far greater happiness and blessing to give than to receive. True Christian living is marked by generous giving rather than grasping.

After finishing his farewell address, Paul knelt down on the ground with all the elders and led them in prayer. Kneeling was the traditional posture of humility and reverence before God. Praying together brought them comfort and placed the future of the church firmly in God's hands.

All the elders broke into loud, deep weeping as they embraced Paul and kissed him goodbye. These tears revealed their immense gratitude and love for the apostle who had spent years caring for their souls. Strong Christian friendships often produce deep, tender emotions when parting.

What grieved the elders most was Paul's clear statement that they would never see his face again in this life. They walked beside him all the way to the water's edge to spend every last second in his company before he boarded the ship. Though they were separated on earth, they rested in the hope of meeting again before the throne of God.
